sources.headline: More than 1,300 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
sources.text: In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture."There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.Nuñez also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France. He said the number of arrests across the country would likely rise.The man in Toulouse, a 20-year-old protester, had several fingers torn off one hand when a nearby explosive went off, Franceinfo reported, citing the medic who treated him.As the unrest continued into the early hours of Sunday morning, authorities in Bouches-du-Rhône, the region in which Marseilles sits, said seven businesses had been "looted or damaged".Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally (RN) party in the north-central city of Orléans, which proceeded peacefully.The recent unrest has played out against a backdrop of a polarised political landscape, with France preparing for what could be the most divisive election period in a generation.Macron will leave office next spring and polls suggest French voters will ultimately face a choice between RN's candidate Marine Le Pen and that of the radical-left La France Insoumise (France Unbowed).Leading figures from both parties have levelled the blame for the disorder at Macron, though right-wing figures have also heaped criticism on rioters while left-wing leaders support the union-led protests.LFI candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon said French media had not covered the peaceful protests while police had created "a setup deliberately designed to provoke chaos" that had "mutilated two people".Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.In Barcelona, more than 120 people were arrested after a student protest descended into what local authorities described as "gratuitous violence". In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.

sources.headline: Macron accused of putting France’s right to protest at risk with ‘vandal’s law’
sources.text: Emmanuel Macron has been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves.The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month of protests in which high-school students have blockaded schools demanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform.Trade unions and gilets jaunes (yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joining sustained street demonstrations in a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of its worst days of violence in years earlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings.The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake of violent clashes after Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was “absolutely essential” after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France.The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis. Marine Le Pen, of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring’s presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police.Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France’s highest court over her conviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds, launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to “bring back order to France”.The RN has claimed the “vandals pay” bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: “Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying.”She said: “We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?”Éric Coquerel, from Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the “vandals pay” law “would mean the end of street demonstrations” in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: “No demonstration could take place again in our country.”In an open letter to Le Monde, leftwing trade unions and France’s Human Rights League wrote: “This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law.”At this weekend’s protests there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested.At demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, from pension changes to same-sex marriage.Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: “Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties.”He said this was “unprecedented” and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law.Lecornu will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades.

sources.headline: The narrative battle over France’s unrest
sources.text:
The Listening PostStudent protests, police violence and French media obsessed with 'barbarians'.What began as protests over education has rapidly taken over the streets of France and turned into one of the country’s biggest waves of unrest in years.Many mainstream media outlets have focused their coverage on the violence and looting rather than on the demands of the demonstrators. A lot of airtime has fixated on who the protesters are and what they look like, often using racist terms. That narrative has been picked up by right-wing movements abroad.Contributors:
Cole Stangler – author, Paris Is Not Dead, and lecturer, American College of the Mediterranean
Diane de Vignemont – Paris-based journalist
Harrison Stetler – lecturer and writer
Philippe Marliere – professor of French and European politics, University College LondonOn our radarIsrael’s elections are just days away and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reverted to a familiar alarmist tactic to consolidate support: hyping an “imminent” threat from Iran and telling the United States that it should “finish the job”. Meenakshi Ravi looks at the messaging.Olga Rudenko: Independent journalism is the ‘ultimate patriotic act’More than four and a half years into Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine remains under attack, and its journalists are forced to balance many responsibilities at once.They are documenting a war that has become more dangerous than ever, countering Russian propaganda efforts and trying to hold their own government to account at a time when the news media have been expected to fall into line. The Kyiv Independent, an online newspaper, has been doing all three since 2021.The Listening Post spoke with its editor-in-chief and cofounder Olga Rudenko about the pressures of reporting when your country is at war.Featuring:
Olga Rudenko – editor-in-chief, The Kyiv IndependentPublished On 25 Oct 2026

More than 1,300 arrests across France as protesters clashed with police
Copyright Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved
By Nathan Rennolds
Published on 25/10/2026 - 9:55 GMT+1•Updated 12:40
Share
Comments
Add Euronews on Google
Some 70,000 law enforcement officers were mobilised ahead of Saturday's planned protests after authorities bolstered security following last weekend's riots.

More than 1,300 people were arrested across France on Saturday as another wave of mass protests swept the country, with more than 400,000 people taking to the streets.

Whilst most demonstrations went ahead peacefully, clashes with police occurred in cities including Paris, Marseilles, Lyon, Bordeaux, Toulouse and Rennes.

In the French capital, a Euronews journalist on the ground saw riot police fire tear gas and charge crowds around Porte de Vincennes on the southeastern edge of the city, whilst some protesters launched fireworks towards officers. Police also deployed a water cannon in an attempt to break up demonstrators and carried out checks of people moving through the nearby Nation square.

Authorities had planned a significantly ramped up security operation following the chaotic scenes that took place across France last weekend, when major cost-of-living protests descended into violence and looting.

Some 70,000 security personnel were mobilised ahead of Saturday's planned protests. Military personnel from Opération Sentinelle were also deployed to help protect key locations and free up police.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez thanked authorities and officers for their work on Saturday but accused "individuals from the far-left and radical far-left" of having "once again sought to sow disorder, especially as the marches were dispersing."

"These acts are unacceptable," he wrote in a post on social media, pointing to locations including Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Grenoble, Nantes, Angers and Lille.

The Yellow Vests movement has called for further demonstrations on 31 October.

To the south of the capital, authorities are also continuing to keep a close watch over the hard-right National Rally party's congress in Orléans, which drew both supporters and counterprotesters on Saturday. On Sunday, the party will hold a major rally to kick off Marine Le Pen's presidential campaign.

According to the Prefecture of the Centre-Val de Loire region and of the Loiret, 3,000 law enforcement and emergency personnel were deployed in Orléans on Saturday as 13,000 demonstrators marched through the city.

sources.headline: Protests roil France once again as police seek to quell violence
sources.text:
Protests roil France once again as police seek to quell violence Hundreds of thousands turned out across France to protest everything from the lack of school funding to economic inequality. Police also were out in force to prevent a repeat of last week's violence.
World
October 24, 20265:21 PM ET
By
Protests roil France once again as police seek to quell violence
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6014520/nx-s1-9977439" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
Hundreds of thousands turned out across France to protest everything from the lack of school funding to economic inequality. Police also were out in force to prevent a repeat of last week's violence.
Transcript
SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: In France today, about 400,000 people came out in cities across the country to demonstrate. The movement began last month with students demanding better facilities. It's now morphed into a broader protest over the high cost of living and social inequality. In response, the French government put in place a massive security operation with more than 70,000 police. NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports.UNIDENTIFIED PROTESTERS: (Chanting in non-English language).ELEANOR BEARDSLEY, BYLINE: Protesters of all ages and backgrounds coursed down a Paris boulevard - students, workers, parents, retirees, and yellow vests, the largely white working-class movement that bedeviled French president Emmanuel Macron in his first term. These left-wing demonstrators held placards calling to tax the rich and for Macron to resign. Dimitry Knoll explains why there is such anger.DMITRY KNOLL: (Speaking French).BEARDSLEY: "We hate Macron," he says, "because he's been leading these ultra-capitalist policies for 10 years that are just widening inequalities, and young people have less hope for the future." Knoll doesn't buy the government's line that France's public debt prevents it from doing more for its people. There's money, he says. It's just in the hands of the rich.SANDRINE DELORIE: (Speaking French).BEARDSLEY: "We pay our taxes, yet everything is declining, and we're giving massive payouts to multinational companies," says Sandrine Delorie. Fellow protester Sarah Meloul says they all deplore the violence, but police aggression fueled it. And sometimes violence is necessary.SARAH MELOUL: (Speaking French).BEARDSLEY: "How did they take the bastille? With violence," she says. The student protests of May '68 succeeded because of violence. Meloul says, the government is finally listening.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: (Speaking French).BEARDSLEY: A different France gathered today 100 miles south of Paris in the town of Orleans, where the far right was holding its annual party Congress.(CHEERING)BEARDSLEY: Polls show far-right leader Marine Le Pen in the lead in next spring's presidential election. That's another reason it's so important to protest, says nurse Jenny Barthelemy.JENNY BARTHELEMY: Well, now it's more dangerous because we've got the national front coming. There's two different Frances. I don't know. I don't know how to explain it. But we're so divided now. I don't know if there's anything to do anymore.BEARDSLEY: There were clashes between small groups of far-left activists and law enforcement in some cities, like Marseilles and Lyon. But with 70,000 police on the streets of France, the government largely avoided a repeat of last week's violence. But tensions are high across the country, and curfews for minors remain in place in many cities. Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.

sources.headline: More than 1,000 arrested in France as protesters and police clash
sources.text:
Updated on: October 25, 2026 / 6:31 AM EDT
/ CBS/AP
Add CBS News on Google
Police made 1,314 arrests in nationwide protests in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said Sunday, after demonstrations over the high cost of living and the country's education system earlier in the day remained largely peaceful. Nuñez 53 officers were hurt in marches. He said on Saturday marches "passed off well" in cities, but police officers found themselves confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from "ultra-left" groups later in the day. Nuñez said some shops and businesses had been looted, but "the scale was far smaller" than a week earlier, when some 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted.He said police acted more rapidly and conducted more pre-demonstration checks. Businesses and shopping centers had also been better protected. Earlier Saturday, the interior minister said police had confiscated weapons including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said. The French Interior Ministry said about 410,000 people participated in about 298 protests around the country. Union organizers from the General Confederation of Labor put the number at around 800,000. An explanation for the discrepancy was not immediately available.
A protester waves the French flag near Porte de Vincennes during a demonstration in Paris on October 24, 2026.
Aris MESSINIS /AFP via Getty Images
Some confrontations were reported between authorities and demonstrators in several cities, but as of Saturday evening there had been no repeat of the major street violence and rioting that erupted amid similar protests last week. Nuñez previously said that French authorities were preparing to maintain order this weekend by maintaining up to 70,000 officers nationwide along with assets including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons. Nuñez said authorities will remain "on high alert" overnight and into Saturday.
Clashes break out in Paris after largely peaceful march Paris had prepared for unrest, with shops boarded up and events including those related to the NFL's first French football game canceled, but authorities described the atmosphere in the city as "calm." Thousands gathered at the Porte d'Italie on the city's southeastern rim for an authorized demonstration. The march had originally been set for the Bastille, near the city's center, and was changed to the more remote Porte d'Italie at the last minute. Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters that it was "scandalous" that Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate," but participants complied with the change.
Protesters march during a demonstration in Paris, Saturday, on Oct. 24, 2026.
Thibault Camus/AP
The front of the march ended without incident. Some chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away from the Porte de Vincennes. Police said 110,000 people participated in the event, while union members put the number at 250,000. As the evening went on, clashes were reported between police and demonstrators, the Agence France-Presse reported. Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists" had "gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters."
Clashes between protesters and police lasted about two hours, he said. The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people, including six minors, were arrested and 40 were placed in police custody. Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offenses or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said. More than 3,000 were stopped and checked by officers, police said.
A protester clashes with police near Porte de Vincennes during a demonstration in Paris on October 24, 2026.
Aris Messinis /AFP via Getty Images
Protesters march against far-right gathering In Orleans, thousands of people marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party. Le Pen is launching her campaign to succeed Emmanuel Macron as France's president. Elections will be held in six months, and surveys show Le Pen is best-placed to win. Demonstrators in Orleans protested both Macron and Le Pen. "Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled, according to the AFP. Police put their numbers at 11,000, while organizers said 26,000 took part. About 50 organizations, including labor unions, left-wing parties and student groups, had called for a protest against Le Pen's nationalist, anti-immigration party.
A crowd marches along a sunken roadway during the cross-party protest against the National Rally in Orleans, France, on Oct. 24, 2026.
Romain Gautier / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images
Some placards seen at the march referenced a shooting in Trappes, a Paris suburb, that left one person dead and several others injured across several locations. Macron called the rampage a "racist terror attack." Prosecutors are investigating the shooting as a terrorist incident. French media reported that the protest against the congress ended peacefully early Saturday afternoon. The gathering is expected to continue through Sunday. Protesters and police clash in smaller cities Demonstrations had been banned in the southeast city of Lyon, but about 150 protesters near the city's center briefly tried to block a road. Police fired tear gas to disperse the group. Tear gas was also used to break up a group of around 1,000 people gathered in the south of the city. Street fires were also reported.
A police helicopter was seen flying over the city, and security forces, armored vehicles and riot police vans were patrolling. A 21-year-old student, who spoke to the Agence France-Presse on the condition of anonymity, described authorities as "really mobile." In the western city of Nantes, thousands of protesters broke through police lines to enter the city center, the AFP reported. Officers used tear gas and a water cannon to try and disperse them. Some on the fringes of the demonstration threw projectiles and aimed fireworks at officers.
French policemen during a demonstration in Lyon, France on October 24, 2026.
Mathieu Prudhomme/Anadolu via Getty Images
Police said about 17,000 attended an event in Marseille. Officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march's endpoint. Street fires were seen in the city. Tear gas was also deployed in Clermont-Ferrand, Bordeaux and Strasbourg, police said. Nuñez said one person was seriously injured in Clermont-Ferrand, but did not provide any details. In the city of Toulouse, a 20-year-old man reportedly had fingers blown off, Nuñez said. He did not provide more details about the person, their condition, or how they came to be injured. Nuñez said that in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier, authorities saw far-right activists who claimed they were there to protect businesses or sought confrontations with "ultra-left militants." He said it was the first time authorities witnessed this phenomenon.
A protester faces police officers in Toulouse, southwestern France on October 24, 2026.
Matthieu Rondel /AFP via Getty Images
In Nice, where demonstrations had also been banned, 11 people were arrested after far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown, regional authorities said. Water cannons were also used in the city.
Organizers call for Halloween demonstrations One group of protesters, the Yellow Vests, said they would hold another round of protests on Oct. 31. The Yellow Vests emerged about eight years ago as a loosely organized group that staged disruptive protests against Macron. Organizers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms." The demonstrations have been ongoing since September, when high school students in the southeast of Paris protested for better conditions. The unrest quickly spread across the country as people took to the streets to demand relief from rising living costs.
A protester holds a French flag during a demonstration against rising living costs in Strasbourg, France, Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026.
Jean-Francois Badias/AP
More protests spread across Europe Other protests took place across Europe on Saturday, encompassing a broad range of issues including pensions, housing costs, anti-war movements, education and corruption.Italian police said in a statement that they carried out nine arrests and briefly detained 371 people during protests in eight cities on Saturday. Of the people who were detained and taken to police stations, 110 were minors, the statement said. Police on Saturday also said they had arrested a 30-year-old man suspected of being the figure behind the "October 17 Movement," a group which had called for the protests.Soldiers were deployed to Milan, the nation's fashion and finance capital, ahead of fresh demonstrations one week after loot

sources.headline: French protest groups demand more rallies as Macron faces tough choices
sources.text: PARIS – French protest groups and unions on Oct 25 called for further demonstrations as they sought to maintain pressure on the government after a huge security operation helped contain unrest during nationwide rallies on Oct 24.The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in the Oct 24 marches as the authorities deployed 70,000 police officers, helping to avert a repeat of the looting and vandalism that swept through many cities on Oct 17.Labour leaders urged further protests on Oct 31 and a nationwide strike on Nov 5, saying frustration over wages, living costs and public services had spread far beyond the student movement that first mobilised in September.Murielle Guilbert, co-leader of the left-wing Solidaires trade union federation, told BFM TV: “We see an aggregation of anger.”She said grievances among students, workers, firefighters and other groups were converging.“We call on people to take to the streets next Saturday.”The SUD Education teaching union said it would join the Oct 31 demonstration, while the large CGT union said it would decide during the week.Macron’s scope to respond is minimalThe Yellow Vests, a grassroots movement that emerged in 2018 as a revolt against fuel taxes, also called for mass rallies on Oct 31, including sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly.“There is anger in this country. It’s growing in schools and universities, on roundabouts, in neighbourhoods, on farms and in workplaces,” activist Azelma Sigaux told reporters.In 2019, President Emmanuel Macron was able to find the resources to reduce fuel costs in response to the Yellow Vests.Seven years on, strained public finances have left him with little room to meet protesters’ demands. His mandate also expires in April 2027, and his centrist party no longer has the majority needed to pass major legislation.The government has begun talks with unions and student representatives to defuse the crisis, but protest leaders say the measures it has proposed so far are inadequate.“We have received no response at all from this government,” Guilbert said.Police unions said on Oct 25 that they did not have enough staff to maintain for any length of time the high level of deployment that on Oct 24, which helped limit disorder to sporadic clashes in a number of cities, including Paris and Marseille.A total of 1,314 people were arrested on Oct 24, half of last week’s numbers, the Interior Ministry said on Oct 25, and about 50 police were injured, compared with more than 1,000 last week.The protests have also resonated beyond France’s borders.On Oct 24, Belgian police used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators.In Albania, peaceful protests that began at the end of May turned into violent unrest in October, and skirmishes have taken place in several Italian cities for a second week running. REUTERS

sources.headline: French protest groups demand more rallies as Macron faces tough choices - Reuters
